before: Scope and denominator. The controllers implement one API application with 23 HTTP method-and-path routes in seven groups: 19 financial routes (accounts 5, journal entries 7, periods 3, reports 4) plus four supporting routes (authentication 1, users 2, audit logs 1). The saved local JMeter load plan contains 12 sampler nodes but only 10 distinct named request types: login, current user, accounts list, journal-entry list and bulk create, period list, and four report reads. These counts describe different units. An OpenAPI import is not proof that every route received equivalent scanner traffic, and the scripted ZAP role probes are a selected subset rather than a complete role-by-route matrix. The October cloud scored mix is separately identified in Section 4.7.
after: Scope and denominator. One API has 23 declared HTTP method/path actions in seven controller groups. The controlled normal and soak scored windows contain nine distinct labels: current user, accounts, journal-entry list, journal bulk write, period list, and four report GETs. The spike peak contains login as a tenth label when additional threads authenticate. The older local JMX has 12 sampler nodes and ten named request types; that inventory is not the scored-cloud denominator. Neither load testing nor importing OpenAPI proves equal coverage of every action and role.

before: Apache JMeter sends concurrent requests and records latency, throughput, and errors. The later cloud experiment in Section 4.7 validated active users, restored the fixture between runs, fixed CPU/RAM limits, and repeated each profile in three pairs. It provides the primary performance result; the older dashboards in Appendix L remain dated local evidence.
after: Apache JMeter sends concurrent requests and records response times, completed-request throughput, and errors. Machine profile IDs p50, p100, and p500 mean 50, 100, and 500 virtual users; p95/p99 are latency percentiles. Sections 4.4 and 4.7 report the controlled cloud experiment with fixed CPU/RAM limits, restored data, validated users, and three alternating pairs per profile. before: Response Time and Throughput: Apache JMeter records average response time, p95/p99 latency, throughput, and errors for the 10 distinct named request types in its saved workload under 50, 100, and 500 VU, soak, and spike profiles. It does not measure all 23 implemented routes or every endpoint under each role.
after: Response Time and Throughput: JMeter 5.5 records p95/p99 latency, completed-request samples per scored second, and errors. The cloud normal/soak mix has nine distinct method/path labels and spike peak has ten including login. The measured sample set is smaller than the 23-action API inventory. Ramp, shutdown and spike-drain periods are excluded from the scored metrics. Spike latency and throughput are reported for the 500-user peak; its error gate covers base, peak and recovery.

before: Resource Utilization: CPU and memory use can affect latency. The 22 September local reproduction did not preserve per-run resource telemetry, so its hardware effects cannot be diagnosed. The later controlled cloud follow-up in Section 4.7 fixed API, SQL, and JMeter CPU/RAM caps and recorded container and host resource summaries.
after: Resource Utilization: the cloud API has 2 CPUs/2 GiB, SQL 2 CPUs/4 GiB (SQL process limit 3,072 MiB), and the separate JMeter generator 4 CPUs/4 GiB with a 2 GiB heap. Host swap is disabled. Host/container CPU, memory, throttling and OOM counters were sampled and retained for every accepted run. SQL throttling is a fraction of quota periods, not ordinary CPU utilization. The older local reproduction lacks equivalent telemetry.

before: Comparison of Performance Metrics: Results from common baseline branch and JMeter remediation branches are compared to determine the impact of ChatGPT (Codex 5.4)’s suggestions on performance, focusing on improvements in response times, error rate reduction, throughput gains, and stability under sustained and spike load conditions.
after: Comparison of Performance Metrics: each of five profiles has three accepted before/after pairs, ordered before/after, after/before, before/after. Each run restores the same backup and starts a fresh API container. A within-run percentile uses the scored request samples; reported side medians and ranges summarize three runs. Paired percentage changes are calculated within each pair and then summarized by their median. They are not ratios of the two side medians. Three pairs provide observed spread, not a claim of statistical significance.

before: How to read the performance evidence. JMeter sends controlled workloads to the API and measures latency, throughput, and errors. The p95 latency is the time below which 95% of measured requests completed, so lower is normally better. Throughput is the number of completed transactions per second, and error rate is the proportion of failed requests. The core 50 VU, 100 VU, and 500 VU profiles determine the primary gate; soak and spike profiles provide additional evidence about sustained and sudden load but cannot override a failed core gate. In this report, 50 VU, 100 VU, and 500 VU name concurrent-user workloads. By contrast, p50, p90, p95, and p99 denote response-time percentiles measured in milliseconds, not percentages.
after: How to read the performance evidence. Sections 4.4 and 4.7 use only the 30 accepted controlled cloud runs. p95/p99 are request-latency percentiles in milliseconds; throughput is scored samples divided by the scored duration; error rate is the proportion of failed samples. Each valid run is assessed against its fixed profile gate. Normal and soak latency uses the hold; spike latency uses the 500-user peak, while recovery is assessed separately. The paired summary retains all three observations, including the extreme but valid 500-user baseline.

before: Observed 22 September local stress-profile result: soak total p95 decreased from 443.95 ms to 171.0 ms and spike total p95 decreased from 33401.75 ms to 4730.85 ms. after: Observed controlled stress result: median soak-hold p95 fell from 685 to 50 ms and median spike-peak p95 from 4,275 to 1,159 ms. All scored errors were zero. Baseline relative-stability gates passed 3/3 in both profiles; after gates passed 1/3 for soak and 0/3 for spike. Lower absolute latency does not cancel the failed relative-stability criteria.

before: Observed 22 September local JMeter core result: 50 VU total p95 increased from 33.0 ms to 199.9 ms, 100 VU increased from 255.9 ms to 1146.9 ms, and 500 VU increased from 106.0 ms to 1547.95 ms. Error rate remained 0.00% for the three core profiles, but the remediation gate failed because 100 VU exceeded 500 ms and 500 VU exceeded 1200 ms.
after: Observed controlled normal-load result: median p95 changed from 161 to 29 ms at 50 users, 670 to 47 ms at 100, and 4,729 to 1,294 ms at 500. After 50/100-user gates passed 3/3; the 500-user p95 gate passed 0/3 because all three after runs exceeded 1,200 ms. Errors were zero in every accepted scored window. Figures L.9–L.11 and L.14–L.16 show the exact per-run values.

before: Concurrency and measurement validity were checked from JMeter thread lifecycle records, JTL bins, logs, and host/container samples. The prescoring p95 gates were 300, 500, and 1,200 ms at 50, 100, and 500 users; the relative soak and spike drift gates were each 20%. These exact limits are study choices. The archived cloud protocol, pair markers, and run summaries preserve the evidence; the raw archive was copied locally before the billable test VMs were deleted.
after: Concurrency validity uses timestamped JMeter thread lifecycle events and JTL activity diagnostics. Host and generator headroom, log errors and OOM/swap counters were also checked. An invalid measurement is EXCLUDED and the complete pair repeated. The final concurrency method is analysis protocol version 2: a post-scoring amendment distinguishes missing request bins from missing users, is disclosed in validity-amendment.md, and was applied to all runs without changing raw timings. Normal p95 limits are 300/500/1,200 ms; error limits 0.5/1/2%. Soak and spike relative p95 limits are 20%, with error limits 1%/3%. Appendix K.4 states the exact windows.

before: Across all 30 accepted cloud runs, minimum host available memory was 5,073.2 MiB, with no observed host swap or container OOM kill. SQL CPU-quota throttling fell sharply but remained 30.66% of scored periods at 500 users after remediation. These resource observations support an account of remaining pressure; they do not isolate a single causal bottleneck or prove longer-term memory safety. The fixed after revision combined report-result reuse, account-ledger caching, removal of report-snapshot writes, and two SQL indexes, so the aggregate gain cannot be assigned to one change.
after: Table 4.8 reports the median across three runs of SQL throttled quota-period fractions and per-container peak RAM as a percentage of each fixed cap. The window is the normal/soak hold or spike peak. Across all 30 accepted runs, minimum host available memory was 5,073.2 MiB, with no observed host swap or container OOM kill. At 500 users, after SQL throttling remained 30.66% of quota periods. These observations do not isolate a causal bottleneck or prove longer-term memory safety. The after revision combines result reuse, account-ledger caching, removal of report-snapshot writes and two SQL indexes, so the combined gain cannot be assigned to one change.
